title: When does a workshop break even?
goal: Build a contribution-margin equation, read its graph, and solve a changed example.

sources.title: Original illustrative example
sources.location: Authored demo; not a real course, assessment or financial forecast.

cues.text: You are running a workshop. Each ticket sells for thirty dollars, but that is not thirty dollars of profit.
The room costs two hundred forty dollars regardless of attendance. These are fixed costs: they do not change with ticket count.
Materials cost ten dollars per attendee. These variable costs increase whenever one more ticket is sold.
Our question is simple: how many tickets cover both the room and the materials, before there is any profit?

steps.title: Ticket price: $30
steps.body: Revenue per ticket, before paying any costs.

steps.title: Fixed cost: $240
steps.body: The room costs the same at zero, six or twelve attendees.

steps.title: Variable cost: $10 per attendee
steps.body: More tickets also mean more materials.

steps.title: Goal: cover all costs
steps.body: Break-even means profit is zero, not revenue is zero.

scenes.title: Let each ticket pay toward the room

cues.text: Start with the price minus the variable cost. Thirty minus ten leaves twenty dollars per ticket to cover the fixed room cost.
Let q mean the number of tickets sold. Twenty dollars times q tickets must equal the two hundred forty dollar room cost.
Divide both sides by twenty. We need twelve tickets. At that point the workshop covers its costs, with zero profit.

steps.note: Contribution per ticket: dollars left after materials.
q is the number of tickets, not a dollar amount.
Twelve tickets cover the fixed cost.

scenes.title: See the same calculation on a graph

cues.text: Now plot money against ticket count. The blue revenue line starts at zero and rises thirty dollars per ticket.
The green total cost line starts at two hundred forty dollars, then rises ten dollars per ticket for materials.
The lines meet at twelve tickets and three hundred sixty dollars. Revenue equals total cost, exactly as the equation predicted.
Beyond twelve tickets, revenue sits above cost. The vertical difference is profit, under these simplified assumptions.

scenes.title: The mistake: treating sales as profit

cues.text: A common mistake is to divide the room cost by the ticket price. That ignores the materials you buy for each attendee.
Use the contribution per ticket in the denominator. Each ticket first pays its variable cost; only the remainder covers fixed costs.
This model assumes fixed prices and costs and enough room for the attendees. A real decision needs those assumptions checked.

steps.title: Do not use 240 ÷ 30
steps.body: A ticket also has to pay for $10 of materials.

steps.title: Use 240 ÷ (30 − 10)
steps.body: Contribution is what remains to cover the room.

steps.title: Check the assumptions
steps.body: Capacity, discounts and changing costs can alter the model.

cues.text: Try this version. Tickets cost thirty five dollars, materials fifteen per attendee, and the room three hundred dollars. How many tickets break even?
First subtract the variable cost from the price. Thirty five minus fifteen still leaves twenty dollars per ticket.
Multiply twenty by the unknown ticket count and set it equal to the new fixed cost: three hundred dollars.
Divide three hundred by twenty. Fifteen tickets are needed. We changed the inputs, but used exactly the same reasoning.

steps.note: Price, variable cost and fixed cost are the givens.
Contribution is twenty dollars per ticket.
Total contribution must cover the fixed cost.

check.question: Why is the ticket price alone the wrong denominator?
check.answer: Each ticket also incurs variable costs. Use price minus variable cost: the contribution toward fixed costs.

cues.text: Separate fixed costs from costs that grow with quantity. That tells you what each sale actually contributes.
Set total contribution equal to fixed cost, then solve for quantity. Use the graph to check what equality means.
Interpret the result in context. Break-even covers costs; it does not promise demand, capacity, or a successful event.

steps.title: 1. Find contribution
steps.body: Price minus variable cost per unit.

steps.title: 3. Interpret and check
steps.body: Confirm units and assumptions before using the result.
